title_original: ‘Sam-Bankman Fried messaged me from prison’: rising star Anthony Boyle on playing the disgraced tech bro – and a zero-hours bike courier
excerpt_original: The actor’s latest roles see him go from a delivery guy on £40 a day to the notorious crypto scammer who stole more than $10bn. His sympathies are clear: ‘I wasn’t brought up to care about money,’ he says In the spring of 2019, Anthony Boyle went to see Cillian Murphy in Grief…

blocks.text: I n the spring of 2019, Anthony Boyle went to see Cillian Murphy in Grief Is the Thing with Feathers at St Ann’s Warehouse in Brooklyn. Afterwards, the 24-year-old actor hung around the stage door. “There were 500 people queueing up for Cillian, but I was the only one who wanted to meet Enda Walsh,” says Boyle, laughing. When the Dublin-born writer Walsh finally appeared, Boyle introduced himself. He was from west Belfast, he’d read Walsh’s plays at drama school, and it was his dream to work with him one day. He asked if Walsh would like to come and see him on Broadway, where he was playing Scorpius Malfoy, son of Draco, in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. How did he respond? Boyle grins. “He was sort of like: ‘Oh.’”

Since Walsh never went to see The Cursed Child, Boyle assumed the writer had immediately forgotten about him. Then, a few years later, he received a letter from Walsh explaining that he was adapting Keiran Goddard’s 2024 novel I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning , about five close friends from a council estate in Birmingham who find themselves questioning everything about their precarious lives as they hit 30. He had scripted the part of Patrick, a politically outspoken graduate working as a zero-hours bike courier to support his young family, with Boyle in mind. Clio Barnard was on board to direct.

links.text: I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning

blocks.text: After meeting Walsh at the stage door, Boyle went away and became one of the most charismatic and watchable actors of his generation. He initially carved out a niche in American televised historical dramas, including The Plot Against America and Masters of the Air before starring in Steven Knight’s House of Guinness last year. In 2024, he was offered the role of IRA veteran Brendan Hughes in the Disney+ drama Say Nothing . Boyle’s initial response was a flat no. “I was like: ‘Disney doing the Troubles? Absolutely not!’ I’d been offered so many jobs about the Troubles, but I didn’t want to be stereotyped as a Belfast lad. I wanted a career that had range. But then I read the book the series was based on and met the author, Patrick Radden Keefe. I realised everyone involved had clear and good intentions. They wanted to show what it was like growing up in Belfast at that time.”

Boyle is fiercely proud of Belfast, referring to it as “the best city in the world”. He grew up in west Belfast and his parents had what he calls “normal people jobs”, his mum working as a receptionist and his dad in security. There’s something elemental about Boyle’s performances on screen and he’s a force of nature in person too; when we meet in central London and sit outside a cafe, he talks with unbridled enthusiasm for more than an hour, often jumping up to make a point. It’s chilly, but he doesn’t seem to notice, even though he’s only wearing a T-shirt and a tracksuit top and thin summer jeans. It’s no surprise when he says that as a kid he used to run into traffic, run up walls, do front flips – “I’m surprised my parents didn’t fill me with Ritalin.”

Expelled from his all-boys Catholic school at 16 for being “disruptive”, he ended up going to a school on the Falls Road – the main artery through west Belfast that is famously decorated with large murals of people such as Bobby Sands, the IRA member who died while on hunger strike – where he was one of a handful of boys among 2,000 girls. He stresses that he was lucky because he was “always allowed to be myself at home; my parents never told me I was stupid or badly behaved”. Later, when he arrived at drama school, he was diagnosed with dyslexia, which made perfect sense.

In the years before he hit his early teens, his kinetic life came to an abrupt halt when he was diagnosed with Perthes disease. A rare condition affecting the hip joint, it lasted several years (he is fine now, although he might suffer from arthritis when he’s older). Often confined to a wheelchair during this period, Boyle would sit by the window at home or in school and watch people, mimicking their voices to while away the hours. This would turn out to be time well spent, since today he has an excellent ear for accents. During this time, he immersed himself in culture, watching films such as Quadrophenia and This Is England and falling hard for the poetry of Seamus Heaney. “I loved the act of reciting poetry and plays. The sense of rhythm and how it dictates your breath and how it makes you feel.” Did he realise he wanted to act? “Yes,” he says, grinning. “I was consumed by the idea.”

When he was 14 or 15, he started acting classes. “My first experience of theatre wasn’t going to the West End in London to see a musical; I saw plays in working men’s bars put on by men who had been in jail for 10 years. One of the first drama classes I took was with a guy who was in the IRA, who’d done drama therapy in jail. We’d act out scenes from his experiences; he’d tell us to play a screw or an IRA member. I didn’t realise that it was an irregular experience. Had I grown up in Oxford, I’d have been doing Shakespeare instead.”

While Boyle is very much part of an excellent ensemble cast in I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning, which also includes Joe Cole and Lola Petticrew, he gives a powerhouse performance as Patrick, who is the film’s conscience. He’s angry at the system, furious at a friend’s betrayal yet tender with his wife Shiv (Petticrew). Boyle has already picked up a best actor award at Rome film festival, and the film is nominated for eight British independent film awards, including best ensemble performance.

He didn’t even have to do a chemistry test with Petticrew, since they grew up together in Belfast. “Lola and I have known each other since we were 11. The first thing we did together was this bizarre production of Romeo and Juliet on a chessboard. That was as close as I got to Shakespeare while growing up,” he says. “I was dressed as Ziggy Stardust, and they were Gene Simmons from Kiss. Lola had to curtsy every time they moved, and I was a knight so I had to move like this.” He jumps up and mimes a weird robotic movement, laughing at his early foray into acting. ‘I think 10 people came and nine walked out. My dad still talks about it now. If I invite him to a premiere, he asks if it’s going to be as bad as that Romeo and Juliet.” Sitting back down, he looks wistful. “Lola is the person who could have been my wife had we both stayed in Belfast. We’re long-term besties.”

Did Boyle and Petticrew learn how to nail the notoriously tricky Brummie accent together? “I went up a few weeks before the other actors. I messaged a bare-knuckle boxer called Ginge on Instagram and asked if we could go for a pint. He introduced me to some locals in Shard End, where the film is shot. I eventually had to brave and try the accent in front of them. Then Lola came up and we walked around the city together. I spoke in the accent, but Lola wasn’t as keen …” Barnard, who “absolutely loved working with Anthony because he’s fearless”, tells me that he “stayed in a Brummie accent throughout filming, so it’s always a surprise to hear his Belfast accent now”.

Boyle doesn’t think he’s particularly method as an actor; it’s a matter of respect: “Patrick is struggling to feed a family of four on £40 a day. Everyone needs to be reminded that people are living like that. It would be something if people see the film and remember to tip their delivery guy. In which case it will have been worth the cringe of doing a Brummie accent.” He grins. “Acting is such an embarrassing job sometimes.”

I See Buildings is a funny but ultimately heartbreaking examination of Thatcher’s cruel legacy. One of Boyle’s upcoming projects is also informed by late-stage capitalism. In the eight-episode Netflix series The Altruists, he plays Sam Bankman-Fried, who founded the FTX cryptocurrency exchange in 2019 before being sentenced to 25 years in prison for fraud, having cheating investors out of more than $10bn. Of course, Boyle went the extra mile for the role, managing to get in touch with Bankman-Fried. “We were messaging on a server that prisoners get access to if they’re well-behaved: I asked him over 100 questions, not all of which he answered. He was very forthcoming and open, but I promised I’d never tell anyone what we discussed.”

Since working on I See Buildings and The Altruists, Boyle has been thinking about power and money: while Patrick can barely feed his family, Bankman-Fried made an estimated $26bn. While he might be empathetic towards Bankman-Fried, his understanding of Patrick is more profound. “Crypto is a million miles away from my life in Belfast. I wasn’t brought up to care about money – for me it’s all about doing good work.” Has he changed since finding success? “Oh God, I hope not! I’m still close with my school mates. I still like to ride horses, swim in the sea, drink pints of Guinness.” He pauses for the first time in an hour. “Oh man, I miss having a good craic in Belfast.”
I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning is in cinemas from 4 December . The Altruists is on Netflix now .
